conventions.convention: State and admissible action sets are finite and nonempty; rewards lie in [0,1]; 0 ≤ γ < 1. The joint next-state/reward kernel permits dependence between its two coordinates.
AC is assumed for infinite trajectory laws and the conditional-expectation suppliers. Finite Bellman maximization uses only finite choice.
Bad times start at t = 1 and use the algorithm's history-conditioned continuation value, with a strict inequality V^{A_t}(h_t) < V*(s_t) − ε. A finite count imposes no prefix condition.
The supplied heuristic satisfies Q* ≤ U ≤ V0 ≤ 1/(1−γ), and the effective cap is Vmax = max{1,V0}.
Each unknown pair has its own absorbing sink; both its entrance reward and sink reward equal (1−γ)q(s,a), giving the unknown pair value exactly q(s,a).
Concentration applies to deterministic sample sizes or fixed-size batches begun at observable histories; it does not assert uniform confidence at a sample size selected after observing its samples.
The escape reduction requires actual fixed-order greedy action selection. Its Q-table cap Qc is distinct from the cap W on unknown-pair values.
Delayed Q-learning succeeds at old value minus batch mean ≥ 2ε1 and replaces the value by batch mean + ε1. The update allowance includes one additional update per pair even at zero heuristic slack.
Positive-tolerance parameter formulas are never evaluated at ε = 0; zero tolerance is treated by separate impossibility and zero-value branches.

load_bearing.statement: Under its stated AC, greedy-action, known-set stability, cap and parameter hypotheses, if simultaneous optimism, policy accuracy and an update-plus-escape bound ζ hold with probability at least 1−ρ, then with probability at least 1−2ρ the PAC-MDP count satisfies N_{4η} ≤ HM, for the displayed q, H and M.

Under AC, independent per-pair potential streams reproduce the interaction's finite-trajectory law. Fixed-size reward means obey 2 exp(−2mx²) tails; empirical transition L1 error has expectation at most sqrt(|S|/m) and upper deviation sqrt(2 ln(1/δ)/m) with failure at most δ. Bounded adapted targets in [0,B] obey the stated martingale-difference tail bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every history-dependent behavior has a trajectory law and a measurable integrable discounted return in [0,1/(1−γ)]. Stationary values satisfy their Bellman equations; the optimality operator is a γ contraction with unique fixed point V*, equal to the supremum over history-dependent behaviors and attained by a deterministic stationary greedy policy.

For its displayed m and β, with probability at least 1−δ, simultaneously at all times the true and empirical trap-model policy values differ by at most η/8, Q approximates the empirical optimum within β, optimism and policy accuracy hold to η, and rebuilds plus outside-known-set selections total at most (m+1)|Eη|.

For the stated batch-size threshold, with probability at least 1−δ all estimates remain optimistic, every attempted update begun outside K succeeds, successful updates total at most G = sum(1+D(s,a)/ε1), and visits outside K total at most 2mG.

With common value cap V and reward/transition errors α, β, stationary-policy and optimal-value errors are at most (α+γVβ)/(1−γ). In its trap-model form, a 2W cap for M1 and γβ ≤ (1−γ)/2 give error at most 2(α+2γWβ)/(1−γ), without a tight cap for M2.

Under AC and the stated information restriction, no finite uniform zero-tolerance bound exists even for one-state two-action Bernoulli bandits at γ=0. Fixed finite legal R-MAX and Delayed Q-learning parameters have the stated infinite-bad-count witnesses; if V* vanishes everywhere, every behavior has N0=0.

concerns.concern: Proof 1.3 writes the Bellman expression T^{π_t}_{M_t}V_t and then takes a maximum difference over states, but V_t has only been defined on the original state set, whereas M_t also contains dedicated absorbing sinks. The immediate completion is to extend V_t to each sink by Q_t(s,a); sink residuals and value differences then vanish. State this extension or explicitly use the reduced operator on original states.

The title, 'A finite bad-step count need not be a permanent stopping time', is ambiguous about the distinction being illustrated. The witness proves that a good step can precede a later bad step; it also has a deterministic permanent good-time threshold n+3. It therefore does not illustrate absence of a permanent stopping time. Clarify the title's intended count-versus-time distinction.
